The karaoke box is where the nameless narrator of Polly Barton’s debut novel feels most like herself – or rather, freest from being herself. Singing alone in Frankfurt, she can be Céline Dion for one song, Whitney Houston the next. She likens singing someone else’s lyrics to prayer or journalling: “Ridiculousness vanished, ownership seemed to vanish: there was only belonging.”

She’s consumed by an obsessive crush on a French co-worker at the videogame translation company where she works – a man she’s never spoken to. Over a year, she watches him from trams and office corridors, building an elaborate fantasy that blurs the line between actual memory and invented encounters.

The novel’s structure follows her fixation. Song titles serve as chapter headings. The book’s title is drawn from Isabella Rossellini’s Seduce Me – short films where she wears paper costumes to perform the courtship rituals of bugs, spiders and sea creatures – which offers a running commentary on human romantic delusion. Like Lorde’s album Melodrama, which chronicles relationships that become far less serious than they seemed, the novel pairs self-aware wit with romantic chaos.

What makes Barton’s approach different is its Moshfegh-like self-awareness. Being let into the narrator’s uncensored thoughts feels like getting a friend’s quadruple texts: “A cliché only seems trite from the outside; on the inside a cliché feels like home. The rogue part spoke like a drunk. It spoke like a dream.” The narrator knows her behaviour is unhinged but can’t stop. Her ex-boyfriend sends her a letter proposing that every man she’s attracted to is a manifestation of a “type”: confident, conventionally masculine men who promise her something different from everything she claims to find wrong about heterosexual romance.

This story is less about romantic obsession than the appeal of temporarily becoming someone else – in karaoke boxes, in translation, in fantasy. The narrator’s real attachment isn’t to a person but to the cruel promise of the crush itself: that this time, this person, this city will finally make her acceptable to herself.

This karaoke is lonely and temporary. She’s still herself when the song ends – it’s enough and it isn’t. For a debut from a Japanese-to-English translator and nonfiction writer, What Am I, A Deer? is confident and serious in its ambition, with an eye for how meaning adapts to the slipperiness of memory, desire and self-knowledge.

Fitzcarraldo, 248pp, $34.99
